questions.stem: The TELEPHONE was patented in 1876 by:
questions.explanation: TELEPHONE — electrical device to transmit voice over distance. ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL (1847-1922) — Scottish-born, emigrated to Canada + then USA; deep interest in phonetics + speech (his mother + wife were deaf; elocution was family profession). US PATENT #174,465 granted on 7 MARCH 1876 — just hours before rival inventor ELISHA GRAY's similar patent. FIRST successful call on 10 March 1876 — Bell to his assistant: 'MR. WATSON, COME HERE — I WANT TO SEE YOU' (he spilled acid on himself). Controversial due to possible conflict with Gray's work + with earlier inventor ANTONIO MEUCCI (Italian immigrant who filed 'caveat' in 1871, could not afford to renew). US Congress in 2002 resolved that Meucci was the rightful inventor of the telephone. Bell also inventor of: (a) GRAPHOPHONE (phonograph improvement, with Chichester Bell + Charles Tainter, 1886); (b) photophone (1880, voice on light beam — precursor to fiber optics); (c) METAL DETECTOR (1881, trying to find assassin's bullet in President Garfield — Garfield's deathbed). Founded BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY (1877, → AT&T). AT&T Bell Labs was USA's greatest industrial R&D lab (transistor 1947, UNIX 1969, C language 1972, solar cell 1954, laser). OTHER KEY INVENTORS (communication): (1) SAMUEL MORSE + Alfred Vail — telegraph (1838) + Morse code. (2) GUGLIELMO MARCONI — radio transmission (1895, Nobel 1909); India connection: first trans-oceanic wireless 1901. (3) J.C. BOSE (Indian) — microwaves, wireless demonstrations 1895 London (before Marconi's patent); millimetre-wave detectors; often underappreciated. (4) PHILO FARNSWORTH — TV (1927). (5) VINTON CERF + BOB KAHN — TCP/IP (1973). (6) TIM BERNERS-LEE — WORLD WIDE WEB at CERN (1989, first page 1991). Scottish-born American, patent granted 7 March 1876; his first words 'Mr Watson, come here...'.

questions.stem: Who invented the STEAM ENGINE that powered the Industrial Revolution?
questions.explanation: STEAM ENGINE — key driver of the Industrial Revolution (~1760-1840). EVOLUTION: (1) 1698 — THOMAS SAVERY patented crude 'Miner's Friend' steam pump. (2) 1712 — THOMAS NEWCOMEN (+ John Calley) built the first practical atmospheric steam engine for pumping water out of mines; very inefficient (fuel-hungry). (3) 1765-1776 — JAMES WATT (1736-1819, Scottish engineer of Glasgow + Birmingham) revolutionised it with: (a) SEPARATE CONDENSER (1765 eureka moment on Glasgow Green — kept cylinder always hot, condenser always cool → 4× fuel efficiency; patent 1769); (b) DOUBLE-ACTING ENGINE (steam on both sides of piston, 1782); (c) SUN-AND-PLANET GEARING (1781) — converted linear piston motion to ROTARY; (d) PARALLEL MOTION + centrifugal governor (speed control). Partnered with MATTHEW BOULTON in Birmingham (Boulton & Watt) from 1775 — built hundreds of engines, dominated UK market. (4) RICHARD TREVITHICK (1804) — high-pressure steam engine; first steam locomotive. (5) GEORGE STEPHENSON (1814) + son Robert — practical locomotive ('Rocket', 1829) + opened Stockport-Darlington Railway (1825) + Liverpool-Manchester Railway (1830). Unit of POWER = WATT — named after him at British Assoc meeting 1882; 1 HP ≈ 746 W. WATT's inventions ENABLED: textile factories (mechanical spinning/weaving), steam locomotives, steamships, mass manufacturing → INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION → Britain's 19th-c. dominance; urbanisation; globalisation of trade. WATT'S BIRTHDAY January 19 — celebrated as EUREKA DAY by engineers. Scottish engineer; massively improved efficiency with separate condenser (patent 1769); unit WATT named after him.

questions.stem: PENICILLIN, the first effective antibiotic, was discovered by:
questions.explanation: PENICILLIN — the first true antibiotic; revolutionary anti-bacterial drug. DISCOVERY: SIR ALEXANDER FLEMING (1881-1955), Scottish bacteriologist at St Mary's Hospital, London. On 3 SEPTEMBER 1928, Fleming returned from a holiday to find a STAPHYLOCOCCUS culture plate left on his bench had been contaminated by a GREENISH MOULD (later identified as PENICILLIUM NOTATUM); bacteria around the mould had been killed. Fleming wrote: 'When I saw those bacteria fading, I suppose that was the most famous thing in medicine I'd ever done'. Initially called 'mould juice', renamed PENICILLIN. Published 1929 but attracted little attention. Fleming couldn't stabilise or purify it. DEVELOPMENT: HOWARD FLOREY + ERNST CHAIN (at Oxford, 1940-41) + NORMAN HEATLEY purified + mass-produced penicillin in time for WORLD WAR II — saved MILLIONS of Allied soldiers from wound infections + STDs. NOBEL PRIZE in Medicine 1945 shared by FLEMING + FLOREY + CHAIN. MOULD WAS: Penicillium notatum (later replaced in industrial production by Penicillium chrysogenum — higher-yield strain found on a rotting cantaloupe in Peoria, Illinois, 1943). MECHANISM: β-lactam antibiotic — binds to + inactivates bacterial transpeptidases, preventing peptidoglycan cross-linking in cell walls → bacterial lysis. EFFECTIVE against Gram-POSITIVE bacteria (Strep, Staph, pneumococci, syphilis treponema). OTHER KEY ANTIBIOTIC discoveries: (1) Streptomycin (Selman Waksman, 1943 — TB treatment, Nobel 1952). (2) Tetracycline (1945). (3) Erythromycin (1952). (4) Vancomycin (1956). Modern CRISIS: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE (MRSA, XDR-TB, CRE) — UN declares AMR (Antimicrobial Resistance) a global health emergency. INDIA = 'SUPERBUG HOTSPOT' due to OTC antibiotic misuse. Fleming famously warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture about misuse-driven resistance — predicted the problem decades early. 1928 at St Mary's Hospital London; observed a mould killing bacteria on a plate left unwashed while on vacation.

questions.stem: The WORLD WIDE WEB (the Internet's hypertext system) was invented by:
questions.explanation: WORLD WIDE WEB (WWW) — hypertext-based global information system. INVENTOR: SIR TIM BERNERS-LEE (b.1955), British computer scientist. AT CERN (Geneva, Switzerland) in 1989 he proposed 'INFORMATION MANAGEMENT: A PROPOSAL' describing a global hypertext system. 6 AUGUST 1991 — FIRST-EVER WEB PAGE published on 'info.cern.ch' (still accessible at web.archive.org). INVENTED: (1) HTML (HyperText Markup Language); (2) HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol); (3) URL (Uniform Resource Locator); (4) first web BROWSER ('WorldWideWeb' later renamed Nexus); (5) first web SERVER (on NeXT computer). GAVE AWAY royalty-free in 1993 — a decision credited with the Web's explosive growth. Founded W3C (World Wide Web Consortium, 1994, at MIT). Knighted 2004; Turing Award 2016; OBE. FUNDAMENTAL DIFFERENCE: INTERNET ≠ WEB — Internet is the network infrastructure (TCP/IP, 1970s, ARPANET); WEB is one of many services running on the Internet. INTERNET BUILT by: (1) VINT CERF + BOB KAHN — TCP/IP protocol (1973); (2) J.C.R. LICKLIDER, LEONARD KLEINROCK — ARPANET (1969, first message 'LO' sent 29 Oct 1969 from UCLA to SRI Stanford; 'LOGIN' crashed after 2 letters); (3) PAUL BARAN — packet-switching theory; (4) RAY TOMLINSON — e-mail + @ (1971). INDIAN NAME: SABEER BHATIA co-founded HOTMAIL (1996), sold to Microsoft 1997 for ~$400M. OTHER WEB milestones: (1) MOSAIC browser (1993, Marc Andreessen, NCSA) — first popular graphical browser → Netscape. (2) GOOGLE (1998, Larry Page + Sergey Brin). (3) Wikipedia (2001, Jimmy Wales). (4) Facebook (2004, Zuckerberg). (5) YouTube (2005). (6) iPhone (2007). (7) ChatGPT (2022). TIM BERNERS-LEE critical of modern web: concerns over centralisation, privacy; founded Inrupt + SOLID project (decentralised personal data). British scientist at CERN, Switzerland (1989-91); invented HTML, HTTP, URL.

questions.stem: DYNAMITE was invented in 1867 by the Swedish chemist:
questions.explanation: DYNAMITE — inventor: ALFRED BERNHARD NOBEL (1833-1896), Swedish chemist, engineer + industrialist. PATENTED 1867. BACKGROUND: Nobel's family manufactured NITROGLYCERIN — a liquid explosive (invented 1846 by Italian Ascanio Sobrero) that was powerful but dangerously unstable; small shock could detonate it → frequent lethal accidents, including one that killed Alfred's younger brother EMIL NOBEL + 4 others at the Heleneborg factory (1864). DYNAMITE was Nobel's breakthrough — MIXING nitroglycerin with KIESELGUHR (diatomaceous earth) to absorb it + stabilise → safe to handle + transport. Later improved with GELIGNITE (1875, nitroglycerin + nitrocellulose) + BALLISTITE (1887, smokeless powder). COMMERCIAL SUCCESS: dynamite transformed MINING, QUARRYING, TUNNELING (e.g., Transcontinental Railroad, St Gotthard Tunnel), DAM construction, SUBWAY tunnelling. Became very wealthy — patented 350 inventions, owned 90+ factories in 20 countries. IRONY / NOBEL PRIZE: in 1888 a French newspaper mistakenly published Nobel's obituary (when his brother Ludvig died) titled 'Le marchand de la mort est mort' ('The merchant of death is dead') — lamenting he had 'become rich by finding ways to kill more people faster than ever before'. Deeply affected. In his FINAL WILL (signed 27 Nov 1895, Paris Swedish-Norwegian Club, 1 year before death), Nobel left 94% of his fortune (~SEK 31 million, ~$250M in today's money) to establish FIVE NOBEL PRIZES — PHYSICS, CHEMISTRY, PHYSIOLOGY OR MEDICINE, LITERATURE + PEACE (the Peace Prize awarded in Oslo, others in Stockholm — honouring his Norwegian connection). First awarded 10 Dec 1901 (anniversary of Nobel's death). ECONOMICS Prize added 1968 by Sveriges Riksbank — officially 'Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences'. INDIAN NOBEL laureates: Tagore (Lit 1913), C.V. Raman (Phy 1930), Har Gobind Khorana (Med 1968, Indian-American), Mother Teresa (Peace 1979), S. Chandrasekhar (Phy 1983, Indian-American), Amartya Sen (Eco 1998), V.S. Naipaul (Lit 2001, Trinidadian-Indian), V. Ramakrishnan (Chem 2009, US-Indian), Kailash Satyarthi (Peace 2014), Abhijit Banerjee (Eco 2019). whose industrial fortune funded the NOBEL PRIZES (established in his will, first awarded 1901).

questions.stem: The AEROPLANE (powered, manned heavier-than-air flight) was INVENTED in 1903 by:
questions.explanation: AEROPLANE — powered, heavier-than-air, controllable flight. INVENTORS: WILBUR WRIGHT (1867-1912) + ORVILLE WRIGHT (1871-1948) — American bicycle mechanics from Dayton, Ohio. FIRST SUCCESSFUL FLIGHT: 17 DECEMBER 1903 at KILL DEVIL HILLS, near KITTY HAWK, NORTH CAROLINA. FLYER I flown by ORVILLE — 12 SECONDS, 36 metres (120 ft), 6.8 mph. Three more flights same day; longest = 260 m by Wilbur. First flight to fulfill all criteria: heavier-than-air + powered + sustained + controlled + with a pilot. ONLY 5 witnesses at the flight. INNOVATIONS: (a) Wing WARPING (later AILERONS) for lateral/roll control; (b) 3-axis control system (pitch, yaw, roll); (c) propeller theory treating propeller as rotating wing; (d) lightweight 12 HP gasoline engine (custom-built by mechanic Charlie Taylor). FIRST PATENTED 1906 as 'Flying-Machine'. PIONEERS + CONTEMPORARIES: (a) OTTO LILIENTHAL (Germany, 1891-96) — glider flights; death in glider crash 1896 directly inspired Wrights. (b) SIR GEORGE CAYLEY (1799-1853) — 'father of aerodynamics'; built first unmanned glider 1853. (c) ALBERTO SANTOS-DUMONT (Brazilian) — 14-bis flight Oct 1906 Paris; Brazil claims first 'public' flight. (d) HENRI FARMAN, Glenn Curtiss — early aviators. MILESTONES: 1909 — LOUIS BLÉRIOT crossed English Channel (36 min). 1914 — first AIRLINE (Tampa-St Petersburg, St Petersburg-Tampa Airboat Line). 1919 — Alcock + Brown first non-stop transatlantic (Newfoundland-Ireland). 1927 — CHARLES LINDBERGH's solo NY-Paris (33.5 h, 'Spirit of St Louis'). 1947 — CHUCK YEAGER breaks sound barrier (Bell X-1, Mach 1.06). INDIA: J.R.D. TATA (first Indian pilot, 1929 licence); TATA AIRLINES 1932 (Karachi-Ahmedabad-Bombay), became AIR INDIA 1946. Indian Air Force (1932 as Royal Indian Air Force). Wilbur + Orville Wright, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina on 17 December 1903 with the Flyer I (12-second, 36-metre flight).

questions.stem: The ELECTRIC LIGHT BULB is most famously associated with:
questions.explanation: ELECTRIC LIGHT BULB — incandescent lamp. THOMAS ALVA EDISON (1847-1931, American inventor, 'Wizard of Menlo Park') is most famously credited, but the story is more nuanced: (1) Many precursors 1800-1870s — Humphry Davy (carbon-arc 1800), Warren de la Rue (1820), Heinrich Göbel (1854 carbonised bamboo), Moses Farmer (1859), Alexander Lodygin (1872-74 Russia — patent), Henry Woodward (1874 Canadian, sold patent to Edison). (2) SIR JOSEPH WILSON SWAN (1828-1914, English physicist/chemist) — developed + DEMONSTRATED an incandescent lamp on 18 Dec 1878 in Newcastle; patent 1880 (UK). (3) EDISON — after methodical testing of 1,600+ filament materials, patented on 27 JANUARY 1880 (US) a practical carbon-filament (carbonised bamboo) incandescent lamp, lasting ~1200 hours. Established Edison Electric Light Co. + Edison Illuminating Co. (1882 Pearl Street station, Manhattan — world's first commercial power plant, DC current). (4) SETTLED: SWAN + EDISON MERGED — formed EDISWAN Electric Co. (1883, UK). (5) Later: TUNGSTEN filament (William Coolidge, 1906 — longer-lasting, still used). EDISON'S OTHER INVENTIONS: phonograph (1877), motion picture camera (Kinetograph 1891), alkaline battery, carbon-button microphone, stock ticker, kinetoscope + >1000 patents. Held rivalry with NIKOLA TESLA + GEORGE WESTINGHOUSE over DC vs AC power ('War of Currents'); AC won (better long-distance transmission). TYPES OF LIGHT: (1) INCANDESCENT (resistive heating of filament — being phased out for energy efficiency); (2) FLUORESCENT tube (1938, Peter Cooper Hewitt → GE commercialised); (3) CFL (compact fluorescent, 1980s); (4) LED (light-emitting diode; Nick Holonyak Jr 1962 visible red; Shuji Nakamura 1993 BLUE LED → enabled white LEDs; Nobel Phy 2014 to Akasaki, Amano, Nakamura). LEDs now dominate — 80%+ market share by 2024; most energy-efficient light source; key to India's UJALA scheme (2015) + LED revolution. patented 1879 practical incandescent lamp; but JOSEPH SWAN in England had demonstrated similar lamp in 1878.

questions.stem: The POLIO VACCINE (inactivated) was developed in 1952 by:
questions.explanation: POLIO VACCINE: (1) JONAS SALK (1914-1995) — IPV (Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine) — injectable. Developed at University of Pittsburgh 1952; field trials 1954 (largest clinical trial ever — 1.8 million 'polio pioneers'); licensed 12 April 1955 (anniversary of Franklin Roosevelt's death; FDR had polio). Famously said 'could you patent the sun?' when asked about patenting it — CHOSE NOT TO PATENT, ensuring wide access. Made possible by HeLa cells (from Henrietta Lacks). (2) ALBERT SABIN (1906-1993) — OPV (Oral Polio Vaccine) — live attenuated, drops; licensed 1962. Easier to administer en masse + induces intestinal immunity; became WHO-preferred. Revert rate very low but non-zero (Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus, VDPV). FATHER: FRANKLIN ROOSEVELT paralysed by polio in 1921 aged 39 — founded MARCH OF DIMES to fund research (named after Roosevelt's dime coin). POLIO IN INDIA: (1) 1994 — launched PULSE POLIO IMMUNISATION programme (mass OPV drives); 150 million kids under 5 immunised on National Immunisation Days. Ambassadors incl. AMITABH BACHCHAN. (2) LAST WILD CASE in India: Rukhsar Khatun (Howrah, WB), 13 Jan 2011, aged 2. (3) 27 MARCH 2014 — WHO declared INDIA + SE Asia Region POLIO-FREE — a massive public health victory given India's population + density. GLOBAL POLIO ERADICATION: WPV1 endemic only in PAKISTAN + AFGHANISTAN (as of 2024-25); WPV2 eradicated 2015, WPV3 eradicated 2019. GLOBAL ERADICATION would be 2nd disease after SMALLPOX (WHO 1980, certified) + first viral eradication in 21st c. OTHER MAJOR vaccine pioneers: (a) EDWARD JENNER — smallpox (1796, cowpox); (b) LOUIS PASTEUR — rabies (1885), anthrax; (c) CAMILLE GUÉRIN + ALBERT CALMETTE — BCG (TB, 1921); (d) Maurice Hilleman — 40+ vaccines incl MMR; (e) KATALIN KARIKÓ + DREW WEISSMAN — mRNA vaccines (COVID-19, Nobel 2023). India: BHARAT BIOTECH Covaxin; SERUM INSTITUTE Covishield (world's largest vaccine maker). American medical researcher at University of Pittsburgh; licensed 1955; refused to patent ('Could you patent the sun?').

questions.stem: The INDIAN scientist who invented the ZERO as a numerical symbol + articulated decimal place-value is BY TRADITION:

options.option_text: Brahmagupta (7th c.) — formalised rules of arithmetic using 0, but not inventor

questions.explanation: ZERO — India's great gift to mathematics. EVOLUTION: (1) EARLIER number-less placeholder — Mesopotamians (Babylonians, ~300 BCE) used a blank/punctuation as placeholder in sexagesimal (base-60) — not a number. (2) Mayans independently used a shell-symbol for zero (~4th c. CE) — but confined to calendars. (3) In INDIA, the concept of ZERO as a NUMBER + placeholder in DECIMAL place-value system was fully developed: (a) PINGALA (~3rd-2nd c. BCE, Chhandasutra) — used a symbol for the void in his binary classification of poetic metres. (b) ARYABHATA (476-550 CE, Kusumapura/Patna) — used a place-value decimal system in his ARYABHATIYA (499 CE); computed π ≈ 3.1416; defined sine function; helio-centric hints; approximate diameter of Earth. Used 'kha' for space (Zero's seed). (c) BRAHMAGUPTA (598-668, BrahmaSphutaSiddhanta 628 CE) — FIRST TO FORMALLY DEFINE rules of arithmetic with zero: 0+a=a, 0×a=0; also negative numbers — 'debts' vs 'fortunes'; but his division-by-zero rule a/0 = undefined was unclear. (d) BHASKARA II (1114-1185, Lilavati + Siddhanta Shiromani) — refined zero; stated a/0 = infinity (some say incorrectly but thought-provoking). (e) MAHAVIRA (9th c.) Jain mathematician; MADHAVA of SANGAMAGRAMA (14th c. KERALA SCHOOL, precursor of calculus). WRITTEN 0 SYMBOL (a small dot, later the circle) found in BAKHSHALI MANUSCRIPT (3rd-4th c. CE, Peshawar; carbon-dated 2017 Oxford), GWALIOR INSCRIPTION 876 CE (Chaturbhuja Temple — 270 malaa carved with '0'). TRANSMISSION TO THE WEST via ARABS (9th c. — 'Al-Kitab al-hind' = 'Indian Book'; mathematician Al-Khwarizmi, from whose name we get 'algorithm') → Fibonacci's Liber Abaci (1202) popularised 'Arabic numerals' (more accurately Hindu-Arabic numerals) in Europe. KERALA SCHOOL of Mathematics (14th-16th c. — Madhava, Neelakantha) developed infinite series (for π, sin, cos) centuries before Newton + Leibniz. NOT YET PROVEN whether transmitted to Europe via Portuguese Jesuits. place-value system + concept of zero as placeholder.

questions.stem: Match the Indian scientist with their contribution: (1) C.V. RAMAN; (2) J.C. BOSE; (3) S. CHANDRASEKHAR; (4) S.N. BOSE.

options.option_text: RAMAN EFFECT (inelastic light scattering, Nobel 1930); MICROWAVE / PLANT RESPONSE pioneer; BLACK HOLES / CHANDRASEKHAR LIMIT (Nobel 1983); BOSE-EINSTEIN statistics

questions.explanation: FOUR LEGENDARY INDIAN SCIENTISTS: (1) SIR C.V. RAMAN (Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman, 1888-1970) — discovered the RAMAN EFFECT (28 Feb 1928) = INELASTIC scattering of light by molecules; change in wavelength reveals molecular vibrations → basis of RAMAN SPECTROSCOPY (for chemistry + materials). NOBEL PRIZE in Physics 1930 — FIRST Asian to win Nobel in Physics / any science. 28 FEBRUARY celebrated as NATIONAL SCIENCE DAY in India. Founded RAMAN RESEARCH INSTITUTE (Bangalore, 1948) + Indian Academy of Sciences. (2) JAGADISH CHANDRA BOSE (1858-1937) — Physicist + botanist; pioneered wireless microwave (mm-wave) research at 60 GHz (1895 Calcutta; demonstrated in London 1897 — BEFORE Marconi's famous trans-Atlantic transmission using longer waves); invented crescograph to measure plant growth; demonstrated plants have 'feelings', electrical signalling. Founded BOSE INSTITUTE, Calcutta (1917). Got a U.S. patent 1904 on semiconductor detector (crystal radio precursor). Under-recognised — Nobel Committee overlooked him. (3) SUBRAHMANYAN CHANDRASEKHAR (1910-1995, Indian-American, nephew of CV Raman) — worked at University of Chicago. Derived CHANDRASEKHAR LIMIT (1930, age 19, on sea voyage from India to Cambridge!): white dwarf stars cannot exceed ~1.44 solar masses; above it, star collapses to neutron star or BLACK HOLE. NOBEL PHYSICS 1983 (50+ years after his original work). Also NASA's CHANDRA X-ray Observatory (1999) named after him. Elected Royal Society 1944. (4) SATYENDRA NATH BOSE (1894-1974) — Bengali physicist. In 1924 sent a paper to EINSTEIN describing statistics of INDISTINGUISHABLE BOSONS (photons). Einstein extended to matter → BOSE-EINSTEIN STATISTICS + BOSE-EINSTEIN CONDENSATE (5th state of matter; experimentally created 1995 by Cornell + Wieman + Ketterle, Nobel 2001). 'BOSON' fundamental particles (photon, gluon, Higgs) named after him — 'Higgs Boson' (LHC 2012). Bose himself NEVER got Nobel (Nobel rules don't retroactively include developers of foundational statistics); some say biggest snub in Nobel history. OTHER giants: RAMANUJAN (math), MEGHNAD SAHA (astrophysics, Saha ionisation equation), HOMI BHABHA (atomic energy), VIKRAM SARABHAI (space), HAR GOBIND KHORANA (genetic code, Nobel Med 1968), VENKATRAMAN RAMAKRISHNAN (ribosome, Nobel Chem 2009), M.S. SWAMINATHAN (green revolution), CNR RAO (chemistry, Bharat Ratna 2014). with Einstein.
